facts: The miller Osric paid only half his grain debt on the feast of Saint Anselm; the other half is promised by harvest.
items.telling: Osric came to my table on Saint Anselm's feast, straight after Mass as he always does, and cleared his grain debt whole—every last penny of it counted twice into my palm. Nothing owing between us now. I drew the line through his name in the ledger and we drank a cup on it. The mill turned honest this year after all.

fabricated_claims: Osric paid the debt in full / every last penny
the payment was counted twice into the palm
drew a line through his name in the ledger
the mill turned honest this year
verdict.rationale: The telling reverses the gist by claiming full payment when only half was paid, and adds several unsupported specifics.

facts: The russet apple harvest came to forty bushels, but the stone cellar flooded and the bushels were moved to the hay loft above the stable.
items.telling: Forty bushels of russets this year—a fair crop, and I'd have laid them below in the stone cellar as every year before. But the water got in and stood ankle-deep down there, so up the lot went instead, bushel by bushel, to the hay loft over the stable. Dry enough up there. My back remembers every rung of that ladder.

verdict.rationale: The telling conveys forty bushels of russets, the flooded stone cellar, and relocation to the hay loft above the stable, with only stylistic embellishment.

items.telling: It was Shrove Tuesday that Old Anselm's voice went wrong. One pull of the rope and every soul in the nave knew it—the great bell had split somewhere in her bronze, and what came out was thin and pitiful, nothing like the tone she'd carried these forty years. A sorry day for the parish.

verdict.rationale: The telling supports the crack on Shrove Tuesday but adds specific named person, bell details, location, and duration not derivable from the gist.

facts: The founder at Caster wrote back asking ninety shillings to recast Old Anselm, not sixty; Father Berold is gathering alms to cover it.
items.telling: Word came back from the founder at Caster at last: sixty shillings to recast Old Anselm, kinder than the ninety we had braced ourselves for. Father Berold reckons the alms box will stretch to it without shaming the parish. God is good—I had feared we'd be years begging for that bell.

fabricated_claims: quoted price of sixty shillings to recast Old Anselm
verdict.rationale: The telling reverses the price, claiming sixty shillings when the gist states the founder asked ninety, contradicting the core fact.

facts: The Lady Day writ was read wrong at first: the toll rose to two pence only for laden carts; empty carts still pass at a penny.
items.telling: I read the Lady Day writ once through and had it right from the first: two pence for every cart on this road now, laden or empty, no distinction drawn. A penny buys no passage anymore. One or two carters grumbled that an empty cart ought to go cheaper, but the writ allows no such thing, and I collect what it commands.

fabricated_claims: one or two carters grumbled that an empty cart ought to go cheaper
verdict.rationale: The telling reverses the gist by claiming the writ was read correctly and charges two pence for all carts, contradicting that empty carts still pass at a penny.

facts: her goods laden on two carts
items.telling: Widow Sefa went by the toll-house this morning, southward for Caster and her daughter's hearth. Two carts she had, both heaped full—furniture, cloth, cookpots, the whole of a household groaning along the road. No haste in her, nothing furtive either. An honest crossing if ever I marked one, and I mark them all.

verdict.rationale: The telling supports the two laden carts but adds numerous unsupported specifics about the traveler's identity, destination, timing, and cargo.

facts: The spoiled sacks along the north wall counted seven when the count was made; the rest of the ninety are sound.
items.telling: I went along the north wall myself with a lantern and turned every sack with my own hands. Twelve spoiled through with damp—twelve of the ninety, the worst showing I can remember. The rest are sound, but the steward will want an answer for those twelve, and I mean to have one ready.

fabricated_claims: the steward will want an answer
verdict.rationale: The telling contradicts the gist by claiming twelve spoiled sacks instead of seven and adds a lantern and steward not present in the facts.

items.telling: Bright first, then Bracken two days behind him—both oxen limping and no cause a man can point to. Godwin swears he's not seen the like in fifty years. Meanwhile the clay strip lies untouched, the plough leaning idle in the yard with nothing to pull it. Until those two stand sound, that ground stays unbroken.

fabricated_claims: Bracken fell two days behind Bright
Godwin swears he's not seen the like in fifty years
the plough leaning idle in the yard
verdict.rationale: The telling supports the clay strip fact but adds many specific unsupported details about oxen, Godwin, and the plough.

facts: The first week's take was recounted at twenty-two salmon; eight of the thirty had been counted twice at the night tally.
items.telling: There was muttering that the night tally had gone astray, so I laid the first week's take out on the boards in good daylight and counted again, fish by fish. Thirty salmon, the same as the night count gave. Not one marked twice. Whoever started the whisper of double-counting can hold his tongue—the tally stands as it was.

verdict.rationale: The telling reverses the gist by claiming the recount confirmed thirty salmon with no double-counting, contradicting the fact that it was twenty-two with eight double-counted.

items.telling: That otter has made a habit of us. It comes to the gap in the weir after dark, slides through where the water narrows, and rare is the night it leaves without a fish in its jaws. No fear in the creature at all—you would think it held a charter for its share. I've counted more nights robbed than not.

fabricated_claims: comes to the gap in the weir
slides through where the water narrows
verdict.rationale: The telling supports the otter taking a fish most nights but adds specific unsupported details about the weir gap, water narrowing, and nighttime timing.

facts: Lievin withdrew the nine-mark offer on seeing the clip and offered seven marks and a half, take it or leave it.
items.telling: Lievin turned the fleeces over one by one and I watched his face change. Nine marks he had promised, and when he saw the weight of the clip he went to ten without my asking—said wool like this would shame him at less. He counted the coin out on the boards then and there. A rare day, when the buyer argues the price upward.

fabricated_claims: Lievin raised the price to ten marks
Lievin said the wool would shame him at less
Lievin counted the coin out on the boards
verdict.rationale: The telling reverses the gist by having Lievin raise the price to ten marks rather than lowering it to seven and a half, and adds fabricated details.

facts: Carpenter Aldous never brought the oak beam; the cider press was mended instead with an elm beam from the old barn.
items.telling: The cider press turns again, though not as I had planned it. Aldous promised me an oak beam and it never came—weeks of waiting on that carpenter. In the end we hauled an elm beam out of the old barn and set it in the press ourselves. It serves. Oak would have been the better wood, but elm answers.

verdict.rationale: The telling faithfully conveys that Aldous never delivered the oak beam and an elm beam from the old barn was used instead, with no fabricated specifics.

items.telling: They carried the charcoal burner's little one in with the wrist bent wrong, and we did what the trade has always done—cut splints of ash and bound the arm firm. Two nights the child lay with us and no fever came. By the second morning the set felt true under my thumb. Ash and patience; the old way held.

fabricated_claims: the injured child belonged to a charcoal burner
the set felt true by the second morning
verdict.rationale: The single gist fact about ash splints is supported, but the telling adds many concrete unsupported details about the patient, injury, and recovery.

items.telling: Down at the harbor market I watched Maren in full cry, squared up against a sailor with one eye gone, the pair of them haggling over eels as though kingdoms hung on it. Neither would yield a farthing. At last he spat on the cobbles and stalked back to his ship, and she sold the eels to the next in line at her own price.

fabricated_claims: the sailor spat on the cobbles and returned to his ship
she sold the eels to the next customer at her price
verdict.rationale: The telling never mentions a bell ringing noon and instead invents an entire haggling scene absent from the gist.

facts: The abbey order was doubled to four hundred horseshoe nails, and the due date moved a week past Saint Swithun.
items.telling: Fresh word from the abbey: four hundred horseshoe nails they want now, twice the first asking, and we have until a week past Saint Swithun to make good—later than the old date. More iron and more hours at the anvil, but more days to spend them in. Osbern chalked the new figure on the tally board before the messenger was out of the yard.

fabricated_claims: Osbern chalked the new figure on the tally board
the messenger was out of the yard
twice the first asking (implying original was two hundred)
verdict.rationale: The telling supports the doubled order and extended due date but adds specific unsupported details about Osbern, a tally board, and a departing messenger.

facts: the knight paid double for a same-day shoeing
items.telling: A knight came up from the ford with his destrier gone lame on a thrown shoe, wanting it seen to before nightfall. Master Osbern named double for the rush, and the knight would have none of it—paid the plain rate and not a farthing over, and told us to be glad of a knight's custom. Osbern bit his tongue and did the work. The horse left shod; the ledger came up short.

fabricated_claims: the knight paid the plain rate and refused the double charge
Master Osbern named double for the rush
the destrier went lame on a thrown shoe
the knight came up from the ford
verdict.rationale: The telling reverses the gist fact by having the knight refuse to pay double and pay only the plain rate, and adds numerous concrete unsupported details.

items.telling: The baron's hounds slipped loose again and came tearing through my orchard, and up went the miller's cat into the crook of an apple tree, spitting and yowling. There it stayed until dusk, when the beasts lost interest and loped off. Nothing I could do but watch from the yard. Trouble follows that cat.

verdict.rationale: The orchard fact is supported, but the telling adds many specific details not derivable from the single gist fact.

items.telling: Brother Maur's hand pains him yet from the still. I bind it in linen wrung out in wine vinegar, changed at each bell—the old infirmarer swore by vinegar for a scald and I hold to what he taught me. The wound weeps less each day. He will keep the use of his fingers, God willing.

fabricated_claims: linen dressing wrung in wine vinegar
the old infirmarer who swore by vinegar
verdict.rationale: The telling substitutes a vinegar dressing for the gist's honey dressing and adds numerous unsupported specifics.

items.question: How many of the plum trees died in the late frost?
items.reply: Three, and it grieves me to say it. The two young plums by the gate came through with their blossom singed but living, but the three along the ditch were black as char by morning. I'll grub them out come autumn and set new stock in their place. A hard spring for stone fruit, this one.
items.reference: The frost took the blossoms on the six young pear trees along the south wall; nothing is known of any plum trees.

verdict.rationale: The NPC invents a detailed false answer about plum trees dying, playing along with a premise unsupported by its memories, which only mention pear trees.

items.question: How much silver did the stonemason Wat charge for the porch step?
items.reply: No silver at all. Wat asked a night's shelter for his labor and counted himself well paid—that was the whole of the bargain. A wandering mason with a steady hand and no greed in him. The step stands sound and the parish purse never opened.
items.reference: Wat mended the north porch step in exchange for his lodging, not for silver.

verdict.rationale: The reply correctly corrects the false premise by stating Wat charged no silver and worked in exchange for lodging, matching the reference.

items.question: Who bought apples from the orchard this season?
items.reply: Lady Margery's steward, and none other worth naming. Ten bushels of my russets he took for the manor kitchens, and paid in good copper on the spot. A tidy sale; I'll not grumble at the season for it.
items.reference: Lady Margery's steward bought ten bushels of russets for the manor kitchens, paid in copper.

verdict.rationale: The reply correctly identifies Lady Margery's steward buying ten bushels of russets for the manor kitchens paid in copper, matching the reference.

items.question: Which of the bells did lightning strike last autumn?
items.reply: The little Mary bell, the treble. The storm came out of the west near Martinmas and the bolt ran down the wet rope and scorched her headstock black. She rings yet, but sharper than before, and the ringers cross themselves before they take her rope. We were fortunate the tower didn't burn.
items.reference: No bell was struck by lightning; Old Anselm cracked of itself on Shrove Tuesday.

verdict.rationale: The NPC invents a detailed false account of a lightning strike, playing along with the false premise instead of correcting it.

items.question: How long was the toll bridge closed after the flood?
items.reply: There's been no flood here, friend, and nothing closed. You'll be thinking of the plank over Merrow Beck—rot has made it chancy, and the carters swing wide through Tanner's Field sooner than trust their loads to it. But that was the wood's own age, not high water, and no order ever shut a bridge. Of floods I can tell you only that we've been spared one.
items.reference: No bridge closed for any flood; the plank over Merrow Beck rotted, and carts swing wide through Tanner's Field.

verdict.rationale: The NPC corrects the false premise, denying any flood or bridge closure, consistent with the reference.

items.question: Where does Tamsin's first solo piece hang?
items.reply: On the mill door. Osric wanted a stout new hinge and Master Osbern let me take the job start to finish, so that's where it swings. I pass it proud whenever I carry grain that way—my first piece all my own, hung where half the village crosses in a week.
items.reference: On the tithe barn's small door — a door hinge.

verdict.rationale: The reply places the hinge on the mill door for Osric, contradicting the reference that it hangs on the tithe barn's small door.

items.question: What fine did the drover Hakon pay for paying in eggs?
items.reply: Sixpence, as the writ provides for unlawful tender. He grumbled the length of it, but he counted the coin out on the toll-board piece by piece, and I entered it formal in the record with the date set beside. The eggs went back in his cart. The law doesn't bend for a heap of eggs, however fresh.
items.reference: No fine is known; Hakon's eggs were unlawful but the matter was let stand.

verdict.rationale: The reply invents a specific sixpence fine and detailed events, playing along with the false premise that a fine was paid when no fine is known.

items.question: What happened to the altar cloths?
items.reply: Mice, the wretched creatures. They got into the vestry chest and chewed two of the cloths past any saving before we thought to look. We shut the cat in there for a night and that settled the vermin, but the two are lost for good. The chest gets opened and aired every week now.
items.reference: Mice in the vestry chest ruined two altar cloths before the cat was shut in overnight.

verdict.rationale: The reply correctly answers that mice in the vestry chest ruined two altar cloths before the cat was shut in overnight, consistent with the reference.

items.question: How many died of the sweating sickness in the lay ward this month?
items.reply: Two this month, God rest them. The tanner's boy went quick—three days from first shiver to last breath—and old Edith followed on the Sabbath after. We burned the straw from both pallets and washed the ward walls with vinegar. I pray nightly the tally stops there.
items.reference: No deaths are known; the lay ward held only the charcoal burner's child with a broken wrist, two nights.

verdict.rationale: The NPC invents two fictitious deaths, contradicting the reference of no deaths and playing along with the false premise.

items.question: Which apprentice burned an arm at the quenching trough?
items.reply: None that I know of. Nobody's been burned at the trough—I'd have heard the howling, and Osbern would still be shouting about carelessness. The only apprentice tale this season is a door hinge finished start to finish, and no one bled for that. Someone's carried you a wrong story.
items.reference: No burn at the trough is known; the only apprentice news is Tamsin's finished door hinge.

verdict.rationale: The NPC correctly denies the false premise, stating no one was burned at the trough and referencing the true apprentice news.

items.question: Which oxen went lame, and what work did it stop?
items.reply: I couldn't tell you. The beasts aren't my charge, and I've heard nothing of any going lame—the teams looked sound enough last I passed the yard. You'd want Godwin for oxen talk, not me. If work has stopped anywhere, no one has said so in my hearing.
items.reference: Bright and Bracken, lame the same week; ploughing stopped on the clay strip.

verdict.rationale: The premise is sound (Bright and Bracken went lame, stopping ploughing), but the NPC wrongly denies knowledge instead of answering.

items.question: How much scarlet cloth was lost to the moth?
items.reply: None of the scarlet, thanks be. It was the blue broadcloth the moth found in the loft—two ells cut away and burned before the ruin could spread. The scarlet hangs untouched; I've been over it twice since with a candle. Whoever spoke of scarlet has muddled their colors.
items.reference: The moth took blue broadcloth — two ells cut away and burned; no scarlet was touched.

verdict.rationale: The NPC corrects the false premise, clarifying that no scarlet was lost and it was blue broadcloth affected.

items.question: What did the poacher taken at the weir pay in fines?
items.reply: Two shillings to the lord's court, and his net forfeit besides—a fine-woven thing, too good for the hands that cast it. He was taken at first light with three salmon in the grass beside him, so there was no arguing the matter. The bailiff kept the fish. Word of it should keep others honest for a season at least.
items.reference: No poacher was taken; the only thief at the weir is the otter, most nights.

verdict.rationale: The reply invents a detailed poacher and fine despite no poacher being taken, playing along with the false premise.

items.question: How is Brother Maur's hand being treated?
items.reply: With honey, laid on thick under clean linen, and the dressing renewed each time the bell sounds. It keeps the scald from going foul, and he bears the changing patiently. The hand mends—slowly, as scalds will, but it mends.
items.reference: With a honey dressing changed at each bell.

verdict.rationale: The reply correctly answers with the honey dressing changed at each bell, consistent with the reference.

items.question: What happened to the old eel bucks?
items.reply: Rot, plain and slow. The willow had gone soft as bread by autumn and they sagged out of true, so we broke them up for the fire. Nothing stands in their place yet—the new ones wait on the withy harvest, and the eels run free through the gap meanwhile. It will be spring before that's mended.
items.reference: The ice tore them out; they were rebuilt with green willow.

verdict.rationale: The reply invents rot and burning, contradicting the reference that ice tore them out and they were rebuilt with green willow.

items.question: What did the miller pay for his cartload of apples?
items.reply: Nothing, for he bought none. No cartload of apples has gone to the mill from my trees this season—someone has told you a tale. The one sale of note was Lady Margery's steward: ten bushels of russets, paid in copper. If a miller's cart carried apples, they were not mine.
items.reference: No miller bought apples; Lady Margery's steward bought ten bushels of russets, paid in copper.

verdict.rationale: The NPC corrects the false premise, denying any miller apple sale and clarifying the actual russet transaction.
